title: Scaling writes: resharding and hot keys
seriesDescription: How to scale write-heavy systems in an interview: vertical scaling and database choice, sharding and partition keys, vertical partitioning, queues and load shedding, batching, hierarchical aggregation, and the resharding and hot-key deep dives.
description: The classic follow-ups: adding shards without downtime and handling a key that is too popular even for a single shard.
source: Study notes: the scaling writes pattern

questions.prompt: Why is "take the system offline, rehash and move everything" a poor way to add shards?

options.text: It means hours of downtime for large datasets.
options.why: Right: production systems migrate gradually.

options.text: Rehashing is impossible with consistent hashing.
options.why: It is possible; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Shards cannot be added to a running system ever.
options.why: They can with the right approach.

options.text: It loses all indexes permanently.
options.why: Not the reason; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: Gradual migration keeps the service available.

questions.prompt: What does the dual-write phase of a live migration do?

options.text: Writes go to both old and new shards while reads prefer the new one, as data moves gradually.
options.why: Right: no data is lost during migration.

options.text: It writes only to the old shard until the migration is over.
options.why: The new shard would miss writes.

options.text: It pauses all reads during the migration for most everyday workloads.
options.why: The aim is no downtime.

options.text: It copies data to a third backup region in a typical production setup.
options.why: Unrelated; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: Once the new shard has caught up, the old location can be retired.

questions.prompt: A viral post receives 100,000 likes per second and even its own shard is overwhelmed. What is the idea?

options.text: Split the key into sub-keys so writes spread over several shards, then sum them on read.
options.why: Right: works for aggregatable data.

options.text: Move the post to a bigger single server only in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Even a dedicated shard may not be enough.

options.text: Reject all likes for that post as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: That loses the data you need.

options.text: Delete the post under normal operating conditions.
options.why: Not a solution; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: This works for counts, views and balances but not for data that must stay atomic, like profiles.

questions.prompt: What is the downside of splitting every key k ways up front?

options.text: The dataset grows k times and every read must visit k sub-keys.
options.why: Right: a big hammer with read amplification.

options.text: The writes become slower on every shard under normal operating conditions.
options.why: Write volume per shard falls.

options.text: Sub-keys cannot be summed.
options.why: They can; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: It requires deleting the primary key as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: Not required; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: If a small k brings writes within capacity, it may still be worth it.

questions.prompt: How does dynamic hot-key splitting differ from splitting every key?

options.text: Only keys detected as hot are split, so cold keys stay cheap to read.
options.why: Right: targeted and cheaper overall.

options.text: It splits keys at random every second in a typical production setup.
options.why: Splits are driven by detection.

options.text: It never needs readers to know anything in the majority of deployments without any extra configuration.
options.why: Readers must agree on which keys are hot.

options.text: It stores each hot key in memory only.
options.why: Unrelated; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: Writers and readers must agree on which sub-keys exist.

questions.prompt: Which approach do most production systems use so readers see all sub-keys?

options.text: Readers always check all sub-keys, accepting read amplification for simplicity.
options.why: Right: simple and easy to understand.

options.text: Writers announce each split and every reader must acknowledge it first for most everyday workloads.
options.why: More complex and less common.

options.text: Readers pick one sub-key at random.
options.why: They would miss counts.

options.text: Readers skip sub-keys and rely on a nightly job under normal operating conditions.
options.why: Counts would be stale.

questions.prompt: Select all kinds of data where key splitting works.

options.text: Like counts.
options.why: Yes: they can be summed.

options.text: View counts.
options.why: Yes: aggregatable; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Account balances kept as additive entries.
options.why: Yes: they can be aggregated.

options.text: A user profile that must be updated atomically.
options.why: No: it cannot be split and summed.

questions.explanation: Atomic data is rarely under the same write pressure.

questions.prompt: True or false: the heart of write scaling is reducing the throughput each individual component has to handle.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: that is the unifying principle.

options.text: False
options.why: It is the unifying principle of the pattern.

questions.explanation: Whether by shards, queues or batches, each component should carry a manageable load.
